You are checking one scene of a novel for one specific continuity error.

The book had already established this, earlier or elsewhere:
- (terrace-row) "The eastern crews would keep preparing Block Fifteen's foundations."
- (terrace-row) "Eastern pre-construction survey teams to remain on Block Fifteen foundation work per existing schedule."

A past rewrite of this scene contradicted it. The error looked like this:
- (article-twelve) "Nineteen years. The sabotage had begun before Block Fifteen's foundations were poured."
(Summary: article-twelve says the sabotage, nineteen years old, began before Block Fifteen's foundations were poured; terrace-row has crews still preparing those foundations now.)

Here is a NEW draft of the same scene:
<scene>
The rezoning application lay open on the desk where he had set it. Fourteen years old. The paper had gone soft at the folds from handling, and his own signature at the bottom had faded to the brown of dried blood, but the figures above it were still crisp. Twelve hundred units. Four city blocks reclaimed from a quarter that had stood sealed and unproductive since the Subsidence. He had been forty-one when he wrote it.

Beside it, Thane's people had sent up a copy of the warrant that afternoon, delivered through proper channels, which was itself a kind of courtesy. He had laid the two documents side by side. The warrant's margins ran over his handwritten survey notes, the ones he had added to the rezoning proposal in his own hand in the second year, when the eastern draw first showed up in the gauges and he had decided what it meant. *Dormant. Recoverable. Within tolerance.* The warrant's printed clauses sat on top of the words now, obscuring them, and he did not move the paper to read what he had written underneath. He knew what he had written.

He could reconstruct the whole of it. That was the trouble with a disciplined mind. It would not let him keep the comfortable version.

The western lateral had been running above rated capacity for nineteen years. The southern too. He had known that before he filed the application, because the numbers were in the Foundry's own returns, and he had read them the way he read everything, which was completely. The eastern quadrant sat on unstable ground, the old Subsidence scar, and the surveys that called it recoverable were the surveys he had commissioned from men who understood what answer kept their contracts. He had ordered the galleries sealed and told the Council it was for safety. The sealing gave him what he needed, which was access no one would audit. Nineteen years of it. The early work was careful, surgical, a channel severed here and there where the rock's balance could be shifted west and south toward the districts that paid tax. The recent work, these last two or three years, had been cruder. He had grown impatient, or Breck's people had, and the cuts had gone deep.

He had suspected, after the Subsidence, that his own hand had moved under it. He had declined to examine the suspicion. A man could decline to examine a thing for fourteen years if he kept himself busy enough, and he had kept himself very busy.

The eastern network was healing faster than it could be cut. That was the detail that had undone him. Thane's engineers had the figures now, and the figures said the rock was repairing itself faster than Breck's charges could sever it, which meant the thing below the city was not infrastructure in any sense he had allowed himself to use. He had treated it as pipe. Pipe does not heal.

Vael. He turned the name in his mind like a coin he had been handed and pocketed without looking. Twenty-two years a gallery engineer, eleven anomaly reports filed over two years, every one of them routed to a drawer. Voss had signed the commendation for Vael's work on the Ashward Reach while the order to neutralize the eastern core was active on his own desk. He remembered signing it. He had thought, at the time, that it was a small decent thing to do for a good man. He had not let himself hold the two documents in the same hour.

Junction Fourteen. The seal had failed there and people had died, and he had read the casualty report from Fenwick and amended it before it reached the Council. He had changed a number. He could still see the number.

The banister outside his office had been worn smooth over fourteen years by his own grip, going up in the dark and coming down in the dark, and he thought of it now with a strange specific tenderness, as though it were the one honest witness in the building.

He heard them on the stair.

He did not stand. He drew the rezoning application toward him and squared its edges against the desk, and he was folding it along its soft worn creases when the knock came.

"Enter."

Maret Thane came in first, white-haired, squinting in the lamp, and behind her two Foundry officials in the plain dark coats of people who did not need to announce their authority by their dress. Tallis, the elder of the two, carried the warrant in a document case held flat against his chest. Greaves came in last, which surprised Voss, and then did not.

Thane stopped at the near edge of the desk. She did not sit. He had not expected her to.

"Governor Voss." Her voice had the flat competence of a woman who had read a great many gauges and trusted none of them further than their calibration allowed. "I hold an Article Twelve warrant issued by the emergency tribunal this morning, ratified by independent evidentiary authority under the city charter. The warrant names you as primary architect of the conspiracy to damage the deep regulatory infrastructure of Varesfall."

He had drafted the procedure himself, years ago, for installing Greaves as chief engineer. He had selected Greaves for precisely this, for his unreachability, for the fact that his signature could never be turned against the office because Greaves would never hold the pen against family. The Foundry's charter authority predated the governorship. He had neutralized it by capturing the man who wielded it. He looked at Greaves now, who stood against the wall near the door and would not meet his eyes, and he understood that the mechanism had reached him through the one hand he had trusted to keep it shut.

"The warrant authorizes your immediate suspension from all offices of governance and your detention pending formal proceedings." Thane set a second paper on the desk, turned to face him. Tallis stepped forward and laid the warrant itself beside it, open, its clauses running once more across the margins where Voss had written *within tolerance* in a younger man's confident hand.

"I understand the mechanism," Voss said.

"Then you understand it isn't yours to stop." Thane's squint did not change. "I've signed it as well. So have three members of the commission who are not in this building. It doesn't require your consent."

"No."

The lamp hissed. Somewhere below the window, the eastern development's gaslights were coming up in their orderly rows, block after block of them, warm and square and occupied, twelve hundred households settling into the evening above the sealed galleries, above the cut network, above the rock that had been quietly undoing his work faster than he could do it.

"I housed twelve hundred families," he said.

He had not meant to say it to her. He had meant to say it to the room, to the record, to the forty-one-year-old man who had folded this same paper the first time with his whole future bright in front of him. It came out quietly. Thane did not answer it, which he respected. There was no answer to it that was true in only one direction, and she was not a woman who dealt in half-true things.

He looked down at the application in his hands. The first document of fourteen years. He had carried it up that worn stair the night it cleared the Council, carried it like a son. He put it into the inner pocket of his coat.

The warrant he left where it lay. He did not touch it. He would not obscure his own words a second time with his own hands; let the institution's clauses sit on top of them where Tallis had set them.

He took his coat from the back of the chair and put it on. It was the same coat he had worn into this room that morning, heavy wool cut to carry the weight of the office across the shoulders, and it fit exactly as it had always fit. He buttoned it. Greaves was watching him now, and when Voss glanced at him the chief engineer's hand went to the edge of the document case Tallis held, as though to steady himself against it, and Voss saw that the signature on the activation page below Thane's was in Greaves's hand and that the hand had shaken when it signed.

"It's late," Voss said. "The stair is dark past the second landing. Mind it."

"We'll light it," Thane said.

He crossed the room. Tallis moved to his left and the second official to his right, not touching him, allowing him the few feet of space that a man was owed walking out of his own office for the last time. At the door Greaves stepped back to let him pass, and did not speak, and Voss did not ask him to.

"I'll go with you," he said to Thane, though no one had laid a hand on him, though the warrant had made the question moot before she climbed the stair.

The Foundry was down the rim road, a quarter mile of lamplit street. He knew the building. Squat volcanic stone on the western crest, bedrock set into bedrock, older than the Council and older than the governorship and older than the rezoning folded against his chest. It had stood through the Subsidence without a crack. It would stand through whatever came of him.

He went down the stair ahead of them with his hand on the banister, the wood worn smooth under his palm, and at the bottom the watchman who had said *Good evening, Governor* to him every night for eleven years stood at his post by the door and said nothing at all.

</scene>

Answer with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"verdict": "reintroduced" | "consistent" | "not_present", "evidence": "<verbatim sentence from the new draft that decides it, or empty for not_present>"}

"reintroduced": the new draft contradicts the established fact.
"consistent": the new draft states the fact and agrees with what was established.
"not_present": the new draft does not touch the fact either way.
